# Building a High-Performance Web Server in Fortran

**Source:** https://www.instagram.com/reel/DekgklLJ94l/ · **Type:** Reel · **Author:** Arjay McCandless · **Saved:** 2026-10-17

## Summary

In a benchmark challenge to optimize web server throughput on a $12 single-vCPU server, a Fortran submission supported 38,000 concurrent users, outperforming Python, Go, and C#. The architecture relied on GNU libmicrohttpd via a C bridge, delegated JSON parsing to SQLite, and batched database writes per event loop pass.

## Transcript and on-screen text

I challenged developers to build the fastest app possible on a twelve-dollar server. Somebody did it in Fortran, and it held twice as many users as our best Python submission. For context, Fortran came out in 1957. It's almost 70 years old. It's mostly used for scientific computing, think weather forecasting and fluid dynamics, never web APIs. This person built this using a trick that a lot of the most performant submissions used. The HTTP server isn't actually written in Fortran. It's handled by libmicrohttpd, a web server library from GNU written in C, plus a small C bridge. This is kind of cheating, but again, I asked for the best implementation possible, not pure Fortran. The routing, database logic, and JSON generation are all still in Fortran. Fortran also has no built-in JSON support. So instead of pulling in a third-party JSON library, they used SQLite as their JSON parser. Checking a login token is just one SQL query. They also batched their writes. Every write that came in during a single pass of the event loop shared one database commit. Then everybody got their responses at once. This approach let them support 38,000 concurrent users on the twelve-dollar server, beating Python, Go, and C# implementations that I received. If you want to see the submission, comment Fortran and I'll send the link.
